paper.title: Reproductive and menopausal factors and risk of systemic lupus erythematosus in women.
paper.abstract:
Objective

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) occurs predominantly in women, and hormones may play a role in its etiology. This study was carried out to examine associations between female reproductive and menopausal factors and the development of SLE.

Methods

A cohort of 238,308 women was prospectively examined. Subjects were older women (ages 30-55 years at start) and younger women (ages 25-42 years at start) from the Nurses' Health Study (NHS) and NHSII cohorts. Incident SLE diagnosed between 1976 and 2003 was confirmed by medical record review. The relative risk (RR) of SLE was estimated separately in each cohort using Cox proportional hazards models, and then pooled using meta-analysis random effects models.

Results

Two hundred sixty-two incident cases of SLE were confirmed among the women. In multivariable models adjusted for reproductive and other risk factors, ageConclusionEarly age at menarche, oral contraceptive use, early age at menopause, surgical menopause, and postmenopausal use of hormones were each associated with an increased risk of SLE. These associations may point to the mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis of SLE.

problem.title: Reproductive and menopausal hormonal factors are linked to increased risk of systemic lupus erythematosus in women
problem.summary: Systemic lupus erythematosus occurs predominantly in women, suggesting a hormonal role in its cause. A large prospective study found that early menarche, oral contraceptive use, surgical menopause, earlier natural menopause, and postmenopausal hormone use were each associated with increased risk of SLE. Age at first birth, parity, and breastfeeding duration showed no association.
problem.affected_women: Women aged 25-55 in the Nurses' Health Study cohorts, particularly those with early menarche, oral contraceptive use, surgical or early menopause, or postmenopausal hormone use

data_need.description: Data on the biological mechanisms linking hormonal exposures (menarche timing, contraceptive use, menopause type, hormone therapy) to SLE pathogenesis is missing
data_need.why_it_matters: Without understanding the underlying mechanisms, it is harder to identify which women are most at risk or to design preventive interventions targeting hormonal pathways.

gap_evidence.note: The authors state that these associations 'may point to the mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis of SLE,' indicating the mechanisms themselves are not established by this study and remain a gap in current understanding.

dataset_source.note: Covers narrative/mechanistic review synthesis and large-cohort epidemiological associations between hormone therapy/menopause and SLE risk, but does not provide definitive experimental or mechanistic (molecular/cellular pathway) proof linking specific hormonal exposures like menarche timing or contraceptive use to SLE pathogenesis; mechanistic causality remains largely inferential.

verification.findings: A search finds a 2022 Frontiers in Medicine review, 'Sex hormones affect the pathogenesis and clinical characteristics of systemic lupus erythematosus,' which synthesizes known immunological and receptor-level mechanisms (estrogen receptor signaling on B/T cells, effects of OCs and HRT) linking hormonal exposures to SLE. There are also newer epidemiological cohort studies, such as a 2024 nationwide Korean cohort study on menopausal hormone therapy and SLE risk and a population-based nested case-control study on HRT and SLE/systemic sclerosis risk. However, these largely quantify associations rather than establishing definitive causal biological pathways, and the review itself notes many relationships (e.g., HRT and disease flare mechanisms) 'have not yet been clarified.'
